pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9-11 (Upper KS2/Grades 4-6): insects as the most successful animals on Earth — ~1 million described species (5–10 million estimated), more than all other animal groups COMBINED. Why so many? Small size (less food needed), fast reproduction (many offspring), flight (reach new habitats), and the versatile exoskeleton.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 Y4 classification / biodiversity; Y6 evolution (why lineages diversify); working-scientifically (interpreting proportion/data).
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-2 (differences in characteristics affect success/reproduction) and biodiversity strands; proportional reasoning with data.
• Operational details — two moves: (a) grasp the staggering PROPORTION (insects vs mammals/birds) — best felt through a to-scale visual, since raw numbers don't land; (b) reason about WHY — link each success factor to a mechanism (small→less food + more niches; fast breeding→rapid adaptation; flight→colonise; exoskeleton→protection + versatility). Note most species are still undiscovered (the estimate gap). Ties classification to biodiversity and success.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9): states insects are the most species-rich group (~1 million known). Tier B (age 10): gives two reasons for their success. Tier C (age 11): compares insect diversity to mammals/birds with a sense of proportion and explains how a success factor (e.g. flight or small size) drives diversification.
bestPractices: Convey the diversity through PROPORTION (to-scale visual) rather than raw numbers, which don't land for children.
Link each success factor to a mechanism (small size→more niches; flight→colonise; fast breeding→rapid adaptation).
Use a striking comparison (beetles alone vs all mammals) to make the magnitude vivid.
Include the discovered-vs-estimated gap so children grasp how much remains unknown.
Connect success to classification and biodiversity, not just a trivia number.
keyRepresentations: A to-scale diversity graphic (groups sized by species count; insects dominant).
A drill-down comparison (beetles vs all mammals).
Four 'why so many?' factor cards with mechanisms.
commonMisconceptions: 'There are more big animals / mammals than insects' — insects vastly outnumber all other animal groups.
'We've discovered nearly all species' — most insect species remain undescribed.
'Success means being big and strong' — here success means species richness and abundance.
'Small size is a weakness' — it's a key reason for insect success.
'All the insect species are just flies and beetles the same' — the diversity is genuinely vast and varied.

learn.summary: For ages 9-11 (Upper KS2 / Grades 4-6): insects are the most species-rich group of animals, with about one million described species (and estimates of several million, often cited as 5-10 million, in total) — more than all other animal groups combined. Learners first grasp the sheer PROPORTION of insect diversity compared with mammals and birds, then reason about WHY insects are so successful by linking each enabling feature (small size, fast reproduction, flight, versatile exoskeleton) to its mechanism. A key distinction throughout: number of SPECIES (kinds) is not the same as number of INDIVIDUALS (abundance). Learners should also meet the discovered-vs-estimated gap, grasping how much remains undescribed.

activities.title: All the animals of Earth, sized by number of species
feedback: If a learner is struck only by the total number, redirect to the comparison: how does the insect area compare in size to the mammal area? Which is the sliver?
If a learner says 'there are more big animals,' point back to the proportions shown — insects vastly outnumber all other animal groups in number of kinds.
Confirm reasoning that uses proportion ('insects are most of the picture; mammals are a thin slice') rather than bare recall.
activities.rationale: The headline insight is a proportion, which children may feel more readily through a to-scale visual than through large numbers alone. An interactive graphic with tappable regions and a beetles-vs-all-mammals drill-down makes the comparison concrete; these interaction examples are optional illustrations, not required features. A fixed, well-chosen graphic can also carry this comparison.
sourceClaims: About one million insect species are described — more than all other animal groups combined — with total estimates of several million; beetles alone are extraordinarily species-rich.
KS2 pupils study classification and biodiversity and interpret data/proportion; Y6 evolution addresses why lineages diversify.
learnerActions: Study a to-scale diversity graphic in which every animal group is sized by its number of species — mammals and birds appearing as thin slivers while insects take up most of the picture (very roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of all described animal species).
Explore the insect region and compare: find that beetles alone outnumber every mammal species put together.
State in your own words how insect diversity compares to mammals and birds, using a sense of proportion rather than just a raw number.
Say roughly what fraction of all animal species are insects, based on what the graphic shows.
activities.intendedInsight: Insects are the most species-rich group of animals; their diversity dwarfs that of mammals and birds. A to-scale visual is intended to make the magnitude land in a way a raw number like '1 million' often does not.

activities.title: Why so many? Linking each feature to its mechanism
feedback: If a learner names a trait but attaches no consequence (e.g. 'they're small' full stop), require the 'so...': why does smallness help there be many kinds?
If a learner restates the fact without a cause ('there are loads because there are loads'), prompt one factor at a time: does being small help? does flying help?
If a learner attaches the wrong consequence to a trait, help re-pair it: small -> little food / many niches; flight -> new habitats; fast breeding -> more variation and splitting into new kinds.
Confirm answers that pair each named feature with how it enables many different kinds.
activities.rationale: Causal reasoning — connecting a feature to the mechanism by which it drives diversification — is the core objective at this age, and requires learners to construct explanations rather than recognise facts. Tappable factor cards or a 'which factor matters most?' toggle are optional ways to surface mechanisms; the essential move is the learner producing the 'so...' explanation.
sourceClaims: Differences in characteristics among individuals affect their ability to survive and reproduce (3-LS4-2), underpinning why some groups diversify.
KS2 pupils study classification and biodiversity and interpret data/proportion; Y6 evolution addresses why lineages diversify.
learnerActions: Take each of four success factors — small size, fast reproduction, flight, and the versatile exoskeleton — and for each one finish the sentence 'and that helps because...'
Small size -> needs little food and fits into countless tiny niches, so many kinds can live in one place (even one tree).
Fast reproduction with many offspring -> populations have lots of variation that selection can act on, so lineages can change and split into new kinds over time.
Flight -> insects reach and spread into new habitats.
Exoskeleton -> tough and versatile, working across many different environments.
Decide which factor you think matters most for producing many KINDS, and explain your reasoning.
activities.intendedInsight: Insect success (species richness) results from features each of which can be tied to a mechanism that lets insects fill a huge variety of niches — not from simply 'being lots.'

activities.title: Species versus individuals: counting kinds, not bodies
feedback: If a learner talks about huge numbers of ants or flies but not about different kinds, name the slip: that is abundance, not diversity — count kinds, not bodies.
Confirm answers that keep species and individuals distinct and apply the right one to 'why so many kinds?'
activities.rationale: A common error is treating 'lots of insects' as meaning lots of individuals of a few kinds. Explicitly contrasting number of species with number of individuals guards against this and sharpens the comparison with mammals and birds.
learnerActions: Compare two statements: 'a million ants in one nest' and 'a million kinds of insect.' Explain how they differ.
State that a nest of a million ants is usually just ONE species, while a million species means a million DIFFERENT kinds.
Discuss whether 'a trillion ants' is the same kind of 'many' as 'a million species' — and why not.
When talking about why there are so many insects, make clear whether you mean many individuals (abundance) or many kinds (diversity).
activities.intendedInsight: Diversity (number of species) and abundance (number of individuals) are different ideas; this topic is about the number of KINDS.

activities.title: How much is still undiscovered?
feedback: If a learner assumes we have found nearly all species, point to the estimate gap: the named million sits inside a much larger estimate.
Confirm reasoning that treats the described count as a lower bound, with many kinds still to be found.
activities.rationale: Including the discovered-vs-estimated gap conveys how much remains unknown and reinforces working-scientifically interpretation of estimates. The exact totals (1 million described; several/5-10 million estimated) should be flagged for source verification.
sourceClaims: About one million insect species are described — more than all other animal groups combined — with total estimates of several million; beetles alone are extraordinarily species-rich.
learnerActions: Consider that about one million insect species have been named, while scientists estimate there may be several million (often cited as 5-10 million) in total.
Estimate roughly what fraction of insect species may still be undescribed.
Explain why this gap means our current count is likely an underestimate of true insect diversity.
activities.intendedInsight: Most insect species are probably still undiscovered; the described million may be only a fraction of the true total.

activities.title: Check and rank the reasoning
feedback: Use the second tier ('how does each reason help?') to separate memorised fact from causal understanding.
Probe further: 'You said insects are small — HOW does being small help there be so many different KINDS?'
Probe with a size contrast: 'What can a tiny beetle do, or cope with, that a big mammal can't, that lets more kinds exist?'
If the learner cannot give a reason or repeats the statistic, build the causal list one factor at a time.
activities.rationale: Ranking, matching and estimating check the facts, while the two-tier open prompt elicits the causal explanation and the species/individuals distinction. Recognition and estimation items assess knowledge but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of the explanation, so at least one open prompt is needed.
learnerActions: Rank several animal groups by number of species, placing insects at the top.

Match each success factor to how it helps (small size <-> needs little food / fits many niches; flight <-> reaches new habitats; fast reproduction <-> more variation and splitting; exoskeleton <-> works in many environments).
Estimate, on a scale, what fraction of all animal species are insects.

Answer the two-tier prompt: 'Scientists have named about a million kinds of insect — far more than all mammals, birds, reptiles and fish combined. Why do you think there are so many different kinds of insect?' then 'How does each reason help insects become so many kinds?'
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner gives reasons tied to how each feature enables diversity and distinguishes species from individuals; a shallow grasp restates the fact, conflates abundance with diversity, or names a feature without a consequence.

constraints: 'Success' here means species richness and abundance, not being big or strong; make this explicit, as children often equate success with size/strength.
Keep number of SPECIES (kinds) and number of INDIVIDUALS (abundance) clearly separated — a recurring misconception.
Ranking, matching and slider/estimate items assess knowledge but do not elicit the learner's own causal explanation; include at least one open prompt requiring constructed reasoning.
Small size is presented as a strength (little food needed, many niches), not a weakness.

A conversational format (e.g. 'ask an entomologist why there are so many beetles') can be engaging, but a spoken exchange describes rather than displays a quantitative proportion; if conveying the scale of insect diversity is the goal, pair any such exchange with a to-scale visual comparison.

Interaction examples (tappable slices, drag-to-compare, discovery-timeline tick-up, factor toggles) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — do not treat them as mandatory, and a well-chosen fixed graphic can also carry the comparison.
Specific totals (~1 million described; several/5-10 million estimated; beetles outnumbering all mammals) should be verified against current authoritative sources before use as exact figures.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row rated 3D as 'poor' with the claim '3D adds no value' and framed the to-scale visual as the only thing that makes the insight land ('does what no number can'); these are catalog preferences, not established pedagogical laws, and have been softened to scoped, qualified proposals.

Exact species counts (~1 million described; estimated 'several million', often cited 5-10 million) and the 'beetles alone outnumber all mammals' comparison are cited to general entomology references marked verified:false; treat as approximate pending verification. The source claim states only 'several million' estimated and does not state the explicit beetles-vs-mammals comparison, so neither the 5-10 million figure nor that comparison is directly attested.

The Y6 'evolution / why lineages diversify' framing justifies the causal 'change and split into new kinds' mechanism; this has been anchored to variation/selection rather than mere population growth, but should still be pitched at an age-appropriate level and not overstated beyond the cited standards.

sourceClaims on the species-vs-individuals activity and the check-and-rank activity were set to [] because no source claim directly supports those teaching/assessment principles (the counts claim supports only the topic).

probeDeeper: 'You said insects are small. HOW does being small help there be so many different KINDS of them?'
'There are far more beetle species than mammal species. What can a tiny beetle do, or cope with, that a big mammal can't, that lets more kinds exist?' (size-contrast counterexample)
'Is "a trillion ants" the same kind of "many" as "a million species"? What's the difference?'
'Which do you think matters most for so many kinds — small size, flight, or fast breeding — and why?'
assess.correctAnswer: There are so many insect species because several features make insects successful. Being small means each one needs very little food and can live in tiny spaces, so many kinds fit in one place. Fast reproduction with lots of offspring means populations grow quickly and can change and split into new kinds over time. Flight lets insects reach and spread into new habitats. The tough, versatile exoskeleton works in many environments. Together these let insects fill a huge variety of niches, which is why there are far more insect species than any other animal group.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses many INDIVIDUALS with many SPECIES — thinks 'lots of insects' means lots of the same few kinds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the two ideas: a million ants in one nest is one species; a million species means a million DIFFERENT kinds. Count kinds, not bodies. Compare '# of species' vs '# of individuals' explicitly.
errorPatterns.distractor: There are lots of insects just because each kind has millions of individuals
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about huge numbers of ants/flies but not about the number of different KINDS; treats abundance and diversity as the same

errorPatterns.pattern: Restates the fact without a cause — 'there are loads because there are loads', names no enabling feature
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt for mechanisms one at a time: does being small help? does flying help? Build the causal list (small, fast-breeding, flight, exoskeleton) and attach a 'so...' to each.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: cannot give a reason, or repeats the statistic when asked why

errorPatterns.pattern: Names a feature but attaches the wrong or no consequence — e.g. 'they're small' without saying why smallness helps diversity
errorPatterns.nextMove: For each named trait, require the consequence: small → needs little food, fits many niches; flight → reaches new habitats; fast breeding → changes and splits into new kinds faster.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists a trait but can't finish 'and that helps because...'; feature floats free of effect

responseLevels.gap: Restates that there are lots of insects with no reason, or confuses many individuals with many species.
responseLevels.full: Gives multiple features AND links each to why it produces so many species (small → many niches/little food; fast breeding → rapid change; flight → spread to new habitats), correctly distinguishing number of species from number of individuals and comparing to mammals/birds.
responseLevels.partial: Names one or two success features (small, flight) but can't explain HOW they lead to many different KINDS, or slips between abundance and diversity.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Scientists have named about a million kinds of insect — far more species than all the mammals, birds, reptiles and fish put together. Why do you think there are SO many different kinds of insect? Give me the reasons, and explain how each reason helps insects become so many kinds.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands insect success gives REASONS tied to how each feature enables diversity (small → little food/many niches; fast breeding → rapid change; flight → spread). A child with a shallow grasp restates the fact ('there are lots because there are lots'), confuses number of INDIVIDUALS with number of SPECIES, or names a feature without linking it to why it creates many KINDS. The second tier ('how does each reason help?') separates causal understanding from a memorised statistic.
